extracted.intended_audience: educated readers of Christian apologetics; skeptics, doubters, and students of natural theology
extracted.subtask_description: An 18th-century natural theology essay arguing for God's eternal existence and attributes from contemplation of the world, the human body, and design-like features; aimed to convince atheists and doubters by stepwise natural-philosophical reasoning and scriptural corroboration.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prove God's eternal existence from the creatures
rubrics_metrics.description: Argue that from the existence and order of created things (even the smallest leaf or grain of sand) one can infer an Eternal Being; if there had been complete Nothing, nothing could ever have come to exist.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Reason that the existence of anything at all (however small) is incompatible with a prior absolute Nothing; show that the visible universe displays order that points to an eternal cause. Cite Romans i.20 as corroboration that 'the invisible things ... are clearly seen' from creation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Begin with humility and invoke divine assistance before enquiry
rubrics_metrics.description: Before proceeding with natural arguments, one should implore the Creator to enlighten understanding and purify the heart, since human reason alone may be dim and prejudiced.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The text recommends prayerful humility as preparation for natural theology: ask God to 'enlighten our Understanding' and 'purify our Hearts' so we may rightly perceive the perfections in creation; this procedural step is presented as necessary for sound contemplation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Contemplate ourselves: use anthro‑pological reflection as evidence
rubrics_metrics.description: Examine one's own constitution (body, faculties, sensations, will) as a witness to wisdom, power, and goodness in a Creator; the contemplation of the human frame yields conviction of purposeful design.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Direct the reader to consider the distinctness of faculties (will, reason, sensation) and the marvel of bodily organization as a first-hand testimonial that points beyond mere chance to a wise maker.

rubrics_metrics.name: Argue that the body is material and cannot think
rubrics_metrics.description: Show experimentally that the body derives from food (earth and water) and that corporeal substance cannot account for understanding, reasoning, or thought.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use examples of nutrition, growth from minute beginnings, and physiological processes to argue that corporeal matter (food → earth/water → body) cannot produce immaterial faculties; this step supports the inference of a non‑bodily soul.

rubrics_metrics.name: Demonstrate the soul as a distinct, thinking substance
rubrics_metrics.description: From the manifest fact that the person understands, reasons, and wills while the body (being material) cannot, conclude that there is another (immaterial) substance — the soul.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The argument: since you know you think, yet your body (derived from earth/water) cannot think, there must be a distinct thinking principle. This is presented as an 'irrefragable Proof' of the soul's existence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Show parents are not the true cause of the person
rubrics_metrics.description: Argue that parents only provide bodily matter and ignorance of detailed formation prevents them from being the true causal origin of the whole person (particularly the soul).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Point out parents' lack of knowledge/control over how bodies are formed (sex, shape, inner structure) and that parental contribution is instrumental, not ultimate; therefore the true cause must be another Being.

rubrics_metrics.name: Establish that our support (life, sustenance) comes from another Being
rubrics_metrics.description: Demonstrate that humans cannot produce or regulate the fundamental conditions sustaining life (sunrise, rain, growth of plants), so our preservation depends on an external being.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ask whether a person can cause the sun to rise or rain to fall or convert food into blood — since they cannot, conclude dependence on a preserver; use this to press moral and practical consequences (obligations to the maker).

rubrics_metrics.name: Dichotomy: the maker either knows or is ignorant (choose a knowing maker)
rubrics_metrics.description: Frame the alternatives: the cause of the world either knows and understands its actions (a God) or is an ignorant chance/necessity; argue that reason and observed order require accepting a knowing Creator.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use thought-experiments (machines, clocks) to show that apparent purposive order cannot plausibly arise from ignorant causes; thus the knowing maker hypothesis is the reasonable choice.

rubrics_metrics.name: Infer attributes of the Maker: wise, mighty, and merciful
rubrics_metrics.description: From the evident skill, provision, and beneficence in nature and the human frame, infer that the maker possesses wisdom, power, and mercy.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Analogize natural objects to well-made machines (watches/clocks) and note that nature's complexity and provision (sun, air, water, organs) far exceed human artificer skill; conclude the maker is supremely wise, powerful, and merciful because of the generous ordering of means for life and enjoyment.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use concrete teleological examples (anatomical particulars) to exhibit design
rubrics_metrics.description: Bring forward particular structures — teeth, enamel, lips, salivary glands, tongue — and show how each is wisely adapted to functions (biting, grinding, speech, moistening, taste), evidencing design.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Describe the form and function of specific organs (e.g., incisors for cutting, grinders for crushing, enamel to prevent decay, glands to moisten food, tongue for speech and swallowing) as micro‑examples of contrivance that support the overall design argument.

rubrics_metrics.name: Appeal to Scripture and conscience as supportive corroboration
rubrics_metrics.description: Bolster natural arguments with scriptural passages (e.g., Romans 1:20, Psalm xiv) and appeals to conscience and common assent among wise men to strengthen conviction.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use biblical testimony that 'the invisible things are clearly seen' from creation and remind the reader that many wise persons have historically depended on these proofs; present this as additional weight, not merely bare natural philosophy.

rubrics_metrics.name: Address the psychological and moral consequences of atheism
rubrics_metrics.description: Argue that atheism leads to unhappiness, continual apprehension, and moral despair, and that recognizing dependence on a benevolent Creator yields peace, gratitude, and hope of eternal happiness.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use rhetorical appeals and anecdote (e.g., a converted atheist lamenting his prior unhappiness) to show the practical value of theistic belief and to motivate honest engagement with the proofs rather than obstinate denial.
